newsitem.title: JAPAN: Dollar falls against yen in Tokyo on trade,rate gap.
newsitem.headline: Dollar falls against yen in Tokyo on trade,rate gap.

text.p: The dollar tumbled against the yen on Monday in Tokyo on the narrowing of the interest rate gap between the United States and Japan, and fears of renewed trade friction between the two countries, dealers said.
At one point the dollar fell to 111.80 yen, its lowest since November 25, 1996, from its close of about 114.38 yen in New York on Friday.

The greenback had recovered slightly by the afternoon to stand just under 113 yen on remarks by Finance Minister Hiroshi Mitsuzuka that stable currency rates are important for Japan to achieve sustainable economic recovery.

"The selling was mostly led by overseas speculators who bought too many dollars over the past several months on expectations of continued capital outflows from Japan into the high-yielding U.S. bond market on the back of wide interest rate gaps between the two nations," said a chief trader at a Japanese long-term credit bank.

However, that view has changed, at least partly, as the likelihood of a U.S. credit tightening in July has begun to recede, suggesting a possible narrowing of the U.S.-Japan interest rate differential, he added.

In New York on Friday, U.S. Treasury yields fell to a three-month low after payrolls expanded by only 138,000 jobs in May after swelling by 323,000 new jobs in April. Economists had anticipated job growth of about 219,000 jobs in May.
The dollar also fell on worries that Japan's April current account surplus data, due to be released on Wednesday, will show a substantial rise, the dealers said.

Japan's current account surplus is expected to rise substantially in April from the year earlier period, due to a drop in imports from sluggish domestic demand after the increase in the consumption tax, economists say.

A Reuters poll of economists showed, on average, that the April current account surplus would grow to 1.13 trillion yen ($10.0 billion), compared with a surplus of 566.6 billion yen ($5.05 billion) last year. The forecasts ranged from 990 billion yen ($8.83 billion) to 1.21 trillion yen ($10.8 billion).
Dealers said overseas speculators were aggressive not just in dollar selling versus the yen, but also dumped substantial amounts of German marks to buy yen.
Japanese institutional investors, such as life insurers and trust banks, also sold dollars to buy yen, but in smaller amounts than the foreign speculators.
